checks.topic: Concept and notation of a limit: definition, one-sided limits and existence, the limit laws and their hypotheses, indeterminate versus infinite forms, continuity and discontinuity

questions.q: The statement lim as x -> 2 of f(x) = 5 means:
options: f(2) is defined and equals 5, so the limit is found by evaluating f at 2
f(x) can be made as close to 5 as we wish by taking x close enough to 2, with x not equal to 2
f(x) approaches 5 as x is taken larger and larger without any bound
f(x) approaches 5 but is never permitted to take the value 5 itself
questions.concept: meaning of a limit
questions.why: Formally: for every epsilon > 0 there is a delta > 0 with 0 < |x - 2| < delta implying |f(x) - 5| < epsilon; the '0 <' is exactly what excludes x = 2. Option 1 confuses the limit with the function value, true only when f is continuous there. Option 3 is the definition of a limit at infinity, not at x = 2. Option 4 adds a prohibition the definition never makes: a constant function equals its limit everywhere.

questions.q: f(x) = x + 1 for every x not equal to 2, and f(2) = 7. Then lim as x -> 2 of f(x) is:
options: 7, since the limit is the value the function takes at the point
3, since the limit depends only on values near x = 2, not at x = 2
non-existent, since f is discontinuous at x = 2 and so has no limit there
3 from the left and 7 from the right, so the two-sided limit fails
questions.concept: limit ignores the value at the point
questions.why: The limit uses values of f at x near but not equal to 2, and every one of those is x + 1, giving 3. Option 1 evaluates instead of taking a limit. Option 3 confuses discontinuity with non-existence of the limit: this is a removable discontinuity, where the limit does exist. Option 4 invents a one-sided split, but both sides use the same formula x + 1.

questions.q: For a function f it is known that lim as x -> 1 from the left of f(x) = 4, lim as x -> 1 from the right of f(x) = 4, and f(1) = 9. Then:
options: lim as x -> 1 of f(x) = 4, and f is discontinuous at x = 1
lim as x -> 1 of f(x) = 9, because the function is actually defined at that point
the limit does not exist, because the one-sided values disagree with f(1)
lim as x -> 1 of f(x) = 4, and f is continuous at x = 1 since the limit exists
questions.concept: three conditions for continuity
questions.why: Both one-sided limits are 4 and agree, so the limit is 4; but f(1) = 9 is not 4, so the third condition of continuity fails and there is a removable discontinuity. Option 2 takes the function value as the limit whenever it exists. Option 3 lets f(a) decide whether a limit exists, which it never does. Option 4 treats 'the limit exists' as the whole of continuity, forgetting that the value must match.

questions.q: Direct substitution into lim as x -> 3 of g(x) produces the expression 7/0. The correct conclusion is:
options: the limit is 0, since dividing by something tiny makes the answer small
the form is indeterminate, so the expression must be factored and cancelled
the form is not indeterminate; |g| grows without bound, so check each side
the limit is 7, since the numerator is what decides the value of the quotient
questions.concept: c/0 is infinite, not indeterminate
questions.why: A fixed non-zero numerator over a quantity shrinking to zero gives quotients of unbounded size, so the limit is +infinity or -infinity, and which one depends on the sign of the denominator on each side, so both sides must be checked (they may disagree, in which case no two-sided limit exists). Option 1 reverses the effect of dividing by a small number. Option 2 is the standard confusion of 7/0 with 0/0; there is no vanishing factor to cancel. Option 4 ignores the denominator entirely.

questions.q: The rule lim as x -> a of [f(x) + g(x)] = lim f + lim g is correctly described by:
options: it holds for any two functions at all, since addition is always permitted
it holds when both separate limits exist; the sum can have a limit when neither does
it holds only when f and g are each continuous at the point x = a
it holds unless one of the two separate limits happens to be equal to zero
questions.concept: hypotheses of the sum law
questions.why: The law needs both separate limits to exist, and it cannot be run backwards: with f = 1/x and g = -1/x at a = 0 neither limit exists, yet f + g = 0 has limit 0. Option 1 drops the hypothesis and licenses that false converse. Option 3 demands continuity, which is sufficient but far stronger than needed. Option 4 imports the non-zero condition from the quotient law, where it belongs to the denominator only.

questions.q: Suppose lim as x -> 1 of f(x) = 0 and lim as x -> 1 of g(x) = 0. Which conclusion do the limit laws justify?
options: lim as x -> 1 of f(x)g(x) = 0
lim as x -> 1 of f(x)/g(x) = 1
lim as x -> 1 of f(x)/g(x) = 0
lim as x -> 1 of f(x)/g(x) does not exist
questions.concept: which law applies when a limit is zero
questions.why: Both limits exist, so the product law gives 0 times 0 = 0. The quotient law does not apply because the denominator's limit is 0, leaving the indeterminate form 0/0. Option 2 is the '0/0 cancels to 1' reflex; take f = 2x, g = x, whose quotient tends to 2. Option 3 is the 'zero on top makes it zero' reflex, ignoring that the bottom also collapses. Option 4 treats indeterminate as synonymous with non-existent, but f = 2x, g = x gives the limit 2.

questions.q: The function f(x) = (x^2 - 1)/(x - 1) at x = 1 has:
options: a removable discontinuity: the limit is 2 but f(1) is not defined
an infinite discontinuity, since the denominator is zero at that point
a jump discontinuity, the one-sided limits there being 1 and -1
no discontinuity at all, since the expression simplifies to x + 1
questions.concept: classifying a discontinuity
questions.why: (x^2 - 1)/(x - 1) = (x - 1)(x + 1)/(x - 1) = x + 1 for x not equal to 1, so the limit is 2 while f(1) is undefined: a hole, repaired by defining f(1) = 2. Option 2 is the reflex that any zero denominator gives an asymptote, but here the zero cancels. Option 3 describes |x - 1|/(x - 1), a different function. Option 4 simplifies and then forgets that x = 1 had to be removed from the domain to do so.

questions.q: The Squeeze theorem lets you conclude that lim as x -> 0 of f(x) = 0 from:
options: f(x) <= x^2 for all x near 0, together with the fact that x^2 -> 0
-x^2 <= f(x) <= x^2 for all x near 0, and both bounds tending to 0
f being bounded near 0, together with some other function tending to 0
f(x) <= g(x) for all x near 0, for some function g with limit 0 at 0
questions.concept: hypotheses of the Squeeze theorem
questions.why: Trapping f between -x^2 and x^2, both tending to 0, forces f to 0. Options 1 and 4 give an upper bound only, under which f could plunge without bound or oscillate below. Option 3 confuses bounded with squeezed: sin(1/x) is bounded near 0 and has no limit there.

questions.q: (explain why) Explain why lim as x -> 2 of f(x) can exist even though f(2) is undefined, and why it can fail to exist even though f(2) is perfectly well defined. Give a short example of each.
questions.concept: independence of limit and value
questions.why: The limit at 2 depends only on f(x) for x close to but different from 2, so f(2) is irrelevant to it. Limit but no value: f(x) = (x^2 - 4)/(x - 2), where f(2) is 0/0 and undefined, but for x not equal to 2 the function equals x + 2, so the limit is 4. Value but no limit: f(x) = 1 for x < 2 and f(x) = 3 for x >= 2, where f(2) = 3 is well defined but the left limit is 1 and the right limit is 3, so no two-sided limit exists. The two ideas are independent, and continuity is exactly the case where both exist and coincide.

questions.q: (explain why) State precisely the condition under which lim as x -> a of f(x) exists, and use it to explain why lim as x -> 0 of |x| exists but lim as x -> 0 of |x|/x does not.
questions.concept: existence via one-sided limits
questions.why: lim as x -> a of f(x) = L if and only if the left limit and the right limit both exist and both equal L. For f(x) = |x|: on the right |x| = x -> 0, on the left |x| = -x -> 0; the two agree, so the limit is 0. For f(x) = |x|/x: on the right |x| = x so the quotient is the constant 1; on the left |x| = -x so the quotient is the constant -1. Both one-sided limits exist but 1 is not -1, so the two-sided limit does not exist, a jump. Nothing here is caused by the denominator being zero; it is caused by the absolute value changing its sign rule at 0.

questions.q: (explain why) Direct substitution can produce 0/0 or it can produce 5/0. Explain what each of these tells you, why only one of them is called indeterminate, and what you should do next in each case.
questions.concept: indeterminate versus infinite forms
questions.why: 0/0 arises when numerator and denominator both vanish at a. It is indeterminate because the answer can be anything: 2x/x -> 2, x^2/x -> 0, x/x^2 -> plus or minus infinity. It never means the limit fails; it means a shared vanishing factor must be removed, by factoring and cancelling, rationalising a surd with its conjugate, combining stacked fractions, or applying L'Hopital's rule. 5/0 arises when only the denominator vanishes. It is not indeterminate: the quotient necessarily grows without bound, so the answer is +infinity or -infinity and the remaining work is a sign check on each side. If the two sides give opposite infinities the two-sided limit does not exist. Factoring and L'Hopital are both wrong moves here; L'Hopital applied to 5/0 returns a finite number that is not the limit.

questions.q: (explain why) State the Squeeze theorem, then use it to explain why lim as x -> 0 of x^2 sin(1/x) = 0, and say why the product law for limits cannot be used to get this answer.
questions.concept: Squeeze theorem applied to a bounded oscillation
questions.why: Statement: if g(x) <= f(x) <= h(x) for all x in some interval around a, except possibly at a itself, and lim g = lim h = L as x -> a, then lim f = L. Application: for every x not equal to 0, -1 <= sin(1/x) <= 1; multiplying through by x^2, which is non-negative and so preserves the inequalities, gives -x^2 <= x^2 sin(1/x) <= x^2. Both bounds tend to 0 as x -> 0, so the middle function is squeezed to 0. Why not the product law: it requires both factors to have limits, and lim as x -> 0 of sin(1/x) does not exist, since 1/x runs off to infinity and the sine oscillates between -1 and 1 without settling. Boundedness of the oscillating factor together with a factor going to 0 is exactly what the Squeeze theorem handles.

checks.topic: Concepts and basic technique: emf versus terminal potential difference, internal resistance and the V-I graph, dimensions of emf, the mechanism of motional emf and Faraday's law, energy density versus total energy in a capacitor, dielectrics, conductors and insulators

questions.q: A cell's emf and its terminal potential difference are numerically equal when:
options: no current is drawn, so nothing is dropped across the internal resistance
the external resistance is very small, so almost all the emf reaches the load
the internal resistance is equal in size to the external resistance
the cell is short-circuited, so the full emf appears across the terminals
questions.concept: emf equals terminal pd only at zero current
questions.why: From emf = V + Ir, setting I = 0 kills the Ir term so V = emf; that is why an open-circuit reading with a high-resistance voltmeter measures the emf. Option b is backwards: a small R means a large current, so Ir is large and V is furthest below emf. Option c is the maximum-power-transfer condition R = r, at which V = emf/2, confused with this question. Option d is the extreme of b: on short circuit V = IR -> 0 and the whole emf is lost internally.

questions.q: Electromotive force is correctly described as:
options: the force, in newtons, that a source exerts on the charge carriers in the circuit
the energy supplied by the source to each coulomb of charge passed through it
the potential difference across the terminals while the circuit is switched on
the current the source drives divided by the total resistance of the circuit
questions.concept: emf is energy per unit charge
questions.why: emf = W/Q, in joules per coulomb, i.e. volts. Option a is the trap laid by the word force: emf has dimensions [M L^2 T^-3 I^-1], not [M L T^-2], and is never quoted in newtons. Option c defines the terminal potential difference, which is smaller than emf whenever current flows. Option d is a mangled Ohm's law and gives amperes per ohm, not volts.

questions.q: The dimensional formula of emf is [M^1 L^2 T^-3 I^-1] because emf is:
options: work divided by current, and work has dimensions [M L^2 T^-2]
work divided by charge, and charge has dimensions [I T]
force divided by charge, and force has dimensions [M L T^-2]
power divided by current squared, as for a resistance
questions.concept: dimensions of emf from work over charge
questions.why: Work = force x displacement = [M][L T^-2][L] = [M L^2 T^-2]; charge = current x time = [I T]; dividing gives [M^1 L^2 T^-3 I^-1]. Option a divides by current alone, losing one power of T and landing on [M L^2 T^-2 I^-1] - the commonest slip, from forgetting that charge is not current. Option c is force per unit charge, which is the electric field. Option d is resistance, [M L^2 T^-3 I^-2], recognisable by the I^-2.

questions.q: The terminal voltage of a cell is plotted against the current drawn. The V-axis intercept and the gradient of the straight line give:
options: the emf and -r
the emf and -R
the internal resistance and -emf
the voltage at maximum current and +r
questions.concept: reading emf and internal resistance off a V-I graph
questions.why: V = emf - Ir is y = c + mx with c = emf at I = 0 and m = -r, so the internal resistance is the magnitude of the negative gradient. Option b confuses internal with external resistance, but R is the quantity being varied to generate the points and so cannot also be the gradient. Option c swaps intercept and gradient, which is dimensionally impossible on a voltage axis. Option d misreads the intercept: I = 0 is the smallest current, not the largest, and a positive gradient would mean the terminal voltage rises under load.

questions.q: A rod slides along rails at speed v in a field B perpendicular to the plane of the circuit. The emf Bvl arises because:
options: the magnetic force does work on the free charges, giving Bvl joules per coulomb
the force qvB drives free charges along the rod until an opposing field balances it
the rod's resistance converts its kinetic energy into electrical energy at the rate Bvl
the circuit's resistance changes as the rod moves, and that change induces a voltage
questions.concept: Lorentz force as the seat of motional emf
questions.why: Each free charge q shares the rod's velocity v, so it feels qvB along the rod; charge piles up at the ends until the electrostatic field it creates balances the magnetic push, and the resulting potential difference per unit charge is Bvl. Option a states the classic error that the magnetic force does the work - a magnetic force is always perpendicular to the charge's velocity and does no net work; the energy comes from the agent pushing the rod. Option c confuses the seat of the emf with dissipation, and Bvl is a voltage, not a rate of energy transfer. Option d blames a changing resistance; what actually changes is the area of the circuit, hence the enclosed flux B l x.

questions.q: In Faraday's law emf = -N dPhi/dt, the minus sign records that:
options: the induced emf is always a negative number, since energy leaves the circuit
the induced emf opposes the change in flux that produced it
the flux through the coil always decreases once an emf has been induced
the emf reverses direction each time the coil completes one full turn
questions.concept: the minus sign is Lenz's law
questions.why: The induced emf, and the current it drives, act so as to oppose the change in flux that created them, which is what makes induction consistent with energy conservation. Option a reads the sign as arithmetic; the sign describes a direction and the magnitude N dPhi/dt is what you quote. Option c confuses opposition to change with opposition to the flux itself: if the flux is falling, the induced current acts to maintain it. Option d describes what a rotating coil in an AC generator happens to do, not what the minus sign means.

questions.q: The expression 1/2 epsilon-0 E^2 gives:
options: the total energy stored in a parallel-plate capacitor, in joules
the energy stored per unit volume of the field, in J/m^3
the work done in carrying unit charge across the plates, in volts
the energy stored per unit area of one plate, in J/m^2
questions.concept: electric field energy density
questions.why: Check the units: epsilon-0 is in F/m and E^2 in (N/C)^2, giving N/m^2 = J/m^3, energy per unit volume. For a parallel-plate capacitor the total is U = 1/2 epsilon-0 E^2 (A d). Option a is the error printed in this week's slides, where 1.77 x 10^-7 J/m^3 is quoted as 1.77 x 10^-7 J; it is out by a factor of the volume. Option c confuses energy per charge (volts) with energy per volume. Option d uses the plate area rather than the volume, so it is out by a factor of d.

questions.q: Which statement about a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium is correct?
options: The field inside is zero, once the free electrons have rearranged to cancel it
The field inside is large, since free electrons are present to carry it
Its resistivity is high, which is what lets its electrons move freely
It has no free electrons, so charge passes straight through it unimpeded
questions.concept: zero field inside a conductor at equilibrium
questions.why: If any field remained inside, the free electrons would still be in motion; equilibrium is precisely the state in which they have stopped, which requires E = 0 inside the material. Option b mistakes the presence of mobile charge for the presence of a field - the mobility is exactly why the field cannot survive. Option c inverts the definition: conductors have low resistivity, insulators high. Option d describes an insulator, and even then charge does not pass straight through - an insulator resists the flow of charge.

questions.q: A student reads 1.5 V across a cell with a high-resistance voltmeter and nothing else connected, then connects a torch bulb and reads 1.2 V. Say what each reading is called, explain where the missing 0.3 V has gone, and state what happens to the second reading if the bulb is replaced by one of lower resistance.
questions.concept: emf, terminal pd and the lost volts Ir
questions.why: The first reading draws essentially no current, so it is the emf: 1.5 V. The second, with the bulb drawing current, is the terminal potential difference: 1.2 V. The missing 0.3 V is the lost volts Ir, the potential difference dropped across the cell's own internal resistance, representing energy per coulomb converted to heat inside the cell rather than delivered to the bulb. From emf = V + Ir, if the bulb draws 0.30 A then r = 0.3/0.3 = 1.0 ohm. Replacing the bulb with one of lower resistance increases the current, since I = emf/(R + r), which increases Ir, so the terminal voltage reading falls further below 1.5 V; in the limit R -> 0 the reading tends to zero.

questions.q: A charged parallel-plate capacitor is disconnected from its battery, and a dielectric slab of constant K is then slid between the plates. Explain what happens to Q, C, V, E and the stored energy U, and explain why the answer for U is different if the battery is instead left connected.
questions.concept: which quantity is held fixed when a dielectric is inserted
questions.why: With the battery disconnected the plates are isolated, so Q is fixed. The dielectric raises the capacitance, C -> KC. Since V = Q/C the voltage falls to V/K, and since E = V/d the field falls to E/K, the polarised dielectric setting up an opposing field that partly cancels the original. The stored energy U = Q^2/(2C) therefore falls to U/K; the energy is not destroyed, since the field pulls the slab in and the missing energy is the mechanical work the field does on the slab. If the battery is left connected the fixed quantity is V, not Q: E = V/d is unchanged, Q rises to KQ, and U = 1/2 C V^2 rises to KU, the battery supplying the extra energy by pushing more charge onto the plates. Same slab, same K, opposite conclusions - so always state which of Q and V is constant before writing anything down.

questions.q: Explain, using units, why 1/2 epsilon-0 E^2 cannot be the total energy stored in a capacitor, and state exactly how it is related to the total energy U for a parallel-plate capacitor of plate area A and separation d.
questions.concept: energy density becomes a total only after multiplying by a volume
questions.why: epsilon-0 is measured in F/m and E in N/C (= V/m), so 1/2 epsilon-0 E^2 has units (F/m)(V/m)^2 = (F V^2)/m^3 = J/m^3, i.e. joules per cubic metre - an energy density, which can never be an energy in joules. For a parallel-plate capacitor the field is uniform between the plates and essentially zero outside, so the total stored energy is the density times the volume it occupies: U = 1/2 epsilon-0 E^2 x (A d), where A d is the volume between the plates. This is the same statement as U = 1/2 C V^2: substituting C = epsilon-0 A/d and V = Ed into 1/2 C V^2 gives 1/2 (epsilon-0 A/d)(Ed)^2 = 1/2 epsilon-0 E^2 (A d). An energy in joules obtained straight from 1/2 epsilon-0 E^2 without multiplying by A d is wrong by exactly that factor.

questions.q: A rod moving on rails in a magnetic field delivers electrical energy to a resistor. Explain why the magnetic field cannot be the source of that energy, identify what actually supplies it, and state the relationship this implies between the force needed to keep the rod moving and the power dissipated.
questions.concept: magnetic forces do no work; the pushing agent supplies the energy
questions.why: The magnetic force on a charge, q v x B, is always perpendicular to that charge's velocity, so it can change the direction of the charge's motion but never do net work on it; a magnetic field cannot be a source of energy. It acts only as an intermediary, separating charge along the rod and thereby setting up the emf. The energy delivered to the resistor comes from the external agent keeping the rod moving at constant speed. Once a current I flows, the field exerts a retarding force F = BIl on the current-carrying rod (Lenz's law again, opposing the motion), so the agent must push with an equal force to hold the speed constant. The mechanical power supplied is therefore Fv = (BIl)v = I(Bvl) = I x emf = I^2 R, exactly the electrical power dissipated. If the agent stops pushing, the retarding force decelerates the rod, its kinetic energy drains into the resistor and the current dies away.

checks.topic: The named computational approaches as concepts: definitions, the three gating factors, and what distinguishes each method from its neighbour

questions.q: The course defines computational approaches to problem solving as approaches that:
options: express solutions to problems in a form that can be run on a computer, using advances such as algorithms, models and simulations
replace human judgement with decisions taken automatically by machine learning systems trained on gathered data
establish whether a problem can be solved by the Universal Turing Machine before any program is written for it
select, among the algorithms already known to work, the one that will run fastest on the available hardware
questions.concept: definition of computational approaches
questions.why: The course wording is that computational approaches express solutions in a form that can be run on a computer, using advances in computing such as algorithms, models and simulations; the definition is about the form the solution takes, not difficulty. Option b mistakes one member of the family (data mining, with machine learning and statistical analysis) for the whole category. Option c imports Week 2 solvability by the UTM, which is a question about problems, not a description of an approach. Option d confuses choosing an approach with tuning efficiency: brute force is in this week's list and is explicitly very slow, so speed cannot be the defining property.

questions.q: Before the decision can be made that computational methods may be used on a problem, the course requires three factors to be considered. Which trio?
options: The nature and parameters are identified; the criteria for success are specified; the problem is grouped as a type
The problem is clearly defined; the problem is computable; the data requirements of the problem are examined
The problem is clearly defined; a null hypothesis is stated; the success criteria for the solution are measured
The problem is computable; an appropriate algorithm is selected; the program is tested before it is released
questions.concept: the three gating factors
questions.why: Clearly defined (current situation, end goal, how to reach it, possible obstacles), computable (are the calculations possible given processing time and capacity), and data requirements examined (data types and storage capacity); only after all three is the decision made. Option a is the trap: those are problem recognition's three factors, which identify the problem rather than decide whether a computer can be used. Options c and d smuggle in later stages, a null hypothesis belonging to hypothesis testing and pre-release testing to performance testing.

questions.q: In that list of factors, 'the problem needs to be computable' means specifically that:
options: the current situation, the end goal and the possible obstacles have all been identified
the required data types and the storage capacity the problem needs have been identified
the required calculations are possible, taking processing times and capacity into account
the problem can be reduced to a more general case for which a solution already exists
questions.concept: computability as a practical gating factor
questions.why: The course states the factor as: determine if the required calculations are possible, considering processing times and capacity. It is a practical question about whether the machine can do the work in a usable time. Option a is the 'clearly defined' factor and option b is the 'data requirements' factor; both are real factors, which is why they mislead here, since the question asks which one this phrase names. Option d is problem recognition's reduction to a more general case.

questions.q: In backtracking, what happens when the algorithm reaches a final state?
options: It saves the result reached at that state so that the same state is never computed a second time
It checks whether the state is accepted or rejected, then returns to a previous state to try untried options
It keeps the option that looked best at each earlier step and discards every option not taken
It divides the states still remaining into smaller sets and solves each of those sets separately
questions.concept: the backtracking mechanism
questions.why: The defining move is to check at a final state whether it is accepted or rejected and then backtrack to a previous state to try other unconsidered options; that reversal is unique to backtracking among this week's methods. Option a is dynamic programming, saving sub-problem results. Option c is the greedy algorithm, committing to the best option at each stage and never revisiting. Option d is divide and conquer. Every distractor names a real method, so the question tests which mechanism belongs to which name.

questions.q: What distinguishes data mining from the other approaches named this week?
options: It starts from a stated prediction and gathers evidence to decide whether that prediction should be rejected
It starts from a set of test scenarios with success criteria and measures a built system against them
It starts from the full space of possible answers and works through all of them until one of them fits
It starts from large volumes of already-gathered data and finds unnoticed patterns and relationships in it
questions.concept: data mining starts from data, not from a question
questions.why: The course defines data mining as extracting valuable information from large data sets through unnoticed patterns and underlying relationships within the data, in order to inform decisions or predict trends; in the music-network example the ratings and shares are already collected and the questions emerge from the data. Option a is hypothesis testing, which runs the opposite way, prediction first and evidence second. Option b is performance testing and option c is brute force. Choosing a means the direction of work, discovery versus verification, needs revising.

questions.q: What distinguishes visualisation from the other computational methods in Lesson I?
options: It is aimed at helping humans, rather than computers, to solve the problem more effectively
It removes the need for the problem to be clearly defined, because the diagram defines it instead
It is the only one of them that examines more than one possible solution before deciding
It illustrates the solution only once the algorithm has produced it, and never beforehand
questions.concept: visualisation serves humans
questions.why: The course says explicitly that visualisation helps humans rather than computers solve problems more effectively, because people process and retain information better as an image than as text. Option b inverts the relationship: a diagram may assist in defining a problem, but the precondition that the problem be clearly defined is not lifted by drawing it. Option c is backtracking's description. Option d misreads the definition, which says visualisation illustrates what a problem entails and how to approach its solution, so it is used before and during the work, as the Dijkstra picture shows.

questions.q: The course attaches a condition to divide and conquer. Which statement expresses it?
options: The solutions of the smaller parts must be stored, so that no part is ever solved a second time
Each smaller part must pass its result to the next part, until the whole task has been completed
At every split, the part that looks most promising is taken and the remaining parts are abandoned
The smaller parts must be simpler than the whole, and combining them less complicated than solving it directly
questions.concept: the two conditions on divide and conquer
questions.why: Splitting is worth doing only if the smaller parts are genuinely simpler than the complex whole and if combining their solutions is less complicated than attacking the original directly; fail either and the split adds work. Option a is what dynamic programming adds on top of splitting, storage of sub-solutions, and is the commonest wrong answer. Option b is pipelining, a chain in which each part feeds the next rather than independent parts recombined. Option c is greedy, and it also contradicts divide and conquer, which abandons nothing: every part must be solved.

questions.q: Performance testing, as the course defines it, is carried out:
options: after release, so that genuine user behaviour rather than simulated behaviour is what gets measured
before release, and what is learned from it is used to make the system or program more effective
only on programs whose data requirements have already been shown to be within storage capacity
whenever a choice must be made between two algorithms that are both known to be correct
questions.concept: performance testing is a pre-release activity
questions.why: The definition is evaluating whether a system or program works as expected or not before it is released, and using that knowledge to make it more effective, by writing test scenarios with success criteria and measuring against them, including erroneous data and simulated real-life circumstances (stress testing). Option a is the misunderstanding that testing means watching live users, which loses both the pre-release clause and the pre-written criteria. Option c invents a dependency on the data-requirements factor. Option d describes comparing two candidates, which is the shape of hypothesis testing with its null hypothesis that the two are equally good.

questions.q: Brute force, greedy and dynamic programming all hunt for a good answer. State what each one does at a decision point, and what each one guarantees. Then say which of the three the course says guarantees that an optimal solution can be found, under what proviso, and why the greedy algorithm carries no such guarantee even though it selects the best option every time.
questions.concept: decision-point behaviour and guarantees of the three search approaches
questions.why: Brute force does not choose at all: it goes through all possible choices until a solution is found, trying every possibility instead of improving efficiency with advanced techniques, and so relies solely on computing power. It cannot miss an existing answer but is simple and consistent yet very slow; a padlock with four digits from 0 to 9 obliges it to face 10000 combinations. Greedy chooses: at each stage it applies the best possible solution available there, always selecting the best optimal path, and never reconsiders, which makes it fast; where greedy solutions are optimal the course says they are always simple and highly efficient, but it might not always produce an optimal solution, because the locally best option can close off a better whole. Dynamic programming breaks the problem into sub-problems and saves their solutions so that no result has to be computed again, and it is the one with the guarantee: provided that a solution to the problem exists, dynamic programming guarantees that an optimal solution can be found, which is why the course says it is mostly used for optimization problems, finding a minimum or maximum. Greedy has no such guarantee precisely because 'best at this stage' and 'best overall' are different quantities: greedy only ever looks at one stage, so it cannot discover that an inferior choice now would pay later.

questions.q: Pipelining and divide and conquer both break a task into parts. State the mechanism of each precisely, and explain the one structural difference between the parts that decides which of the two approaches a given task fits.
questions.concept: dependent chain versus independent parts
questions.why: Divide and conquer first splits a complex problem into smaller easier parts; each part is then solved, and the solutions of the parts give the solution of the whole. The parts are the same kind of problem in smaller form (merge sort splits a list into lists), they can be worked independently, and there is a combining step at the end (the merge). It is subject to its two conditions: the parts must be simpler than the whole and combining must be less complicated than solving the original directly. Pipelining divides a task into a series of subtasks where each subtask leads to the next; each subtask is executed by a different process in a series, and the result of one process feeds into the next, repeated until the whole task is finished, as when one function's output is the next function's input or an order total is produced by summing product costs and then adding VAT. The structural difference is dependency between the parts. In divide and conquer the parts do not need one another's results and could be solved in any order, so a combining step is required; in pipelining each part cannot start until the previous one has finished, because the previous output is its input, and no combining step exists because the last stage already holds the answer. So: smaller copies of the same problem that must be recombined means divide and conquer; different stages forced into a fixed order because each consumes what the one before produced means pipelining.

questions.q: The word 'criteria' appears in two of the week's methods: problem recognition specifies 'the problem requirement or criteria for success', and performance testing sets 'success criteria' for its test scenarios. Explain what each set of criteria is for, at what point in the work each is written, and what goes wrong if a team writes only the second.
questions.concept: criteria for success in problem recognition versus in performance testing
questions.why: In problem recognition, specifying the problem requirement or criteria for success is one of the three factors, alongside identifying the nature and parameters of the problem and determining whether it can be grouped as a specific type, and its purpose is to ensure the proposed solution will deal with the root cause of the problem. These criteria are written at the very beginning, before anything is built, and they define what would count as having solved the problem. In performance testing, the success criteria accompany a set of test scenarios, and their purpose is to let the team measure the system or program against them before release so that what is learned can make it more effective; erroneous data and simulated real-life circumstances are the standard scenarios. These criteria are written after there is something to test, and they define what would count as the program behaving as expected. A team that writes only the second has criteria for whether the program does what it was built to do but none for whether that was the right thing to build: the program can pass every scenario and still leave the root cause untouched, because nothing ever recorded what the problem required. That is the failure problem recognition exists to prevent.

questions.q: Define null hypothesis, significance level and p-value as the course states them, give the accept/reject rule, and explain what the course says rejecting the null hypothesis does NOT prove. Use the course's own example of comparing method A with method B.
questions.concept: null hypothesis, significance level, p-value and the accept/reject rule
questions.why: A hypothesis is a tentative, intelligent guess about the solution to the problem: a specific statement of prediction describing in concrete terms what you expect to happen, and an assumption that can be tested and proved right or wrong. The null hypothesis is the initial assumption to be tested: comparing method A with method B to determine whether both are good, the initial assumption that both methods are equally good is the null hypothesis, and the task becomes determining whether it is true or not. The significance level is the probability of rejecting the null hypothesis when it is true; a level of 0.05 means a 5 percent risk of concluding that something exists when it does not. The p-value is a number between 0 and 1 describing how likely it is that the null hypothesis is true, and the smaller the p-value the stronger the evidence that you should reject the null. The rule: when the p-value of the data is less than or equal to the significance level the null hypothesis is rejected, and when the p-value is higher than the significance level the null hypothesis is accepted. The caution: rejecting the null hypothesis does not prove that something does not exist, it only means the evidence is not enough. A rejection is a statement about the strength of evidence at the level chosen, not a proof about the world, and a stricter significance level might not have licensed it at all.

checks.topic: Evaluating limits algebraically: multi-step problems with factor-and-cancel, conjugates, stacked fractions, one-sided and infinite limits, limits at infinity with surds, piecewise matching and repeated L'Hopital

questions.q: lim as x -> 2 of (x^3 - 8)/(x^2 - 4) equals:
options: it does not exist
questions.concept: factor and cancel with a difference of cubes
questions.why: Substitution gives 0/0. x^3 - 8 = (x - 2)(x^2 + 2x + 4) and x^2 - 4 = (x - 2)(x + 2); cancelling (x - 2), legal because x is never 2 inside the limit, leaves (x^2 + 2x + 4)/(x + 2) -> 12/4 = 3. Option 2 comes from mis-factoring the cubes as (x - 2)(x^2 + 4), giving 8/4 = 2; revise a^3 - b^3 = (a - b)(a^2 + ab + b^2). Option 1 reads 'numerator -> 0 so the answer is 0', ignoring that the denominator also collapses. Option 4 treats the form 0/0 as proof that the limit fails.

questions.q: lim as x -> 0 of (sqrt(x + 9) - 3)/x equals:
options: it does not exist
questions.concept: rationalising with the conjugate
questions.why: Multiplying top and bottom by (sqrt(x + 9) + 3) makes the numerator (x + 9) - 9 = x, so the expression is x/[x(sqrt(x + 9) + 3)] = 1/(sqrt(x + 9) + 3) -> 1/6. Option 3 comes from multiplying only the numerator by the conjugate, or cancelling x from the top twice, which doubles the result. Option 1 takes the vanishing numerator as the whole story. Option 4 mistakes 0/0 for non-existence.

questions.q: lim as x -> 3 from the left of (x + 1)/(x - 3) is:
options: +infinity
-infinity
questions.concept: sign analysis of an infinite one-sided limit
questions.why: Substitution gives 4/0, so this is a sign question, not an algebra question. As x -> 3 from the left, x < 3, so x - 3 is a small negative number while the numerator tends to 4 > 0; positive over small-negative is large negative, so the limit is -infinity. Option 1 is the answer from the right-hand side, where x - 3 is small positive. Option 4 substitutes into the numerator only. Option 3 inverts the effect of dividing by a quantity approaching zero.

questions.q: lim as x -> -infinity of sqrt(9x^2 + 1)/(x + 2) equals:
questions.concept: sqrt(x^2) = |x| = -x when x is negative
questions.why: Write sqrt(9x^2 + 1) = |x| sqrt(9 + 1/x^2). Dividing numerator and denominator by x and using |x|/x = -1 for x < 0 gives -sqrt(9 + 1/x^2)/(1 + 2/x) -> -3. Option 1 is the same computation with |x| replaced by x, the commonest sign error in limits at infinity, and it is correct only as x -> +infinity. Option 4 takes the square root of 9x^2 as 9x, dropping the root. Option 3 applies 'the denominator wins' without comparing growth: the numerator behaves like 3|x|, so the two match.

questions.q: lim as x -> infinity of (sqrt(x^2 + 3x) - x) equals:
options: infinity
questions.concept: infinity minus infinity handled by a conjugate
questions.why: Multiplying by (sqrt(x^2 + 3x) + x) over itself gives (x^2 + 3x - x^2)/(sqrt(x^2 + 3x) + x) = 3x/(sqrt(x^2 + 3x) + x); dividing top and bottom by x gives 3/(sqrt(1 + 3/x) + 1) -> 3/2. Option 1 treats infinity minus infinity as 0, the classic misreading of an indeterminate form as a cancellation. Option 4 assumes the surd grows faster than x, but they grow at the same rate and only the lower-order difference survives. Option 2 forgets to divide the surd by x, leaving 3/1.

questions.q: lim as x -> 0 of [1/(x + 2) - 1/2]/x equals:
options: it does not exist
questions.concept: stacked fractions combined over a common denominator
questions.why: The numerator is [2 - (x + 2)]/[2(x + 2)] = -x/[2(x + 2)], so the whole expression is -x/[2x(x + 2)] = -1/[2(x + 2)] -> -1/4. Option 1 loses the minus sign when subtracting (x + 2) from 2. Option 3 substitutes into the numerator alone and sees 0. Option 4 treats 0/0 as failure. As a check, this limit is the derivative of 1/x at x = 2, namely -1/x^2 = -1/4.

questions.q: f(x) = ax + 1 for x < 3 and f(x) = x^2 - 2 for x >= 3. lim as x -> 3 of f(x) exists exactly when a is:
options: no value of a makes it exist
questions.concept: matching one-sided limits at a piecewise joint
questions.why: Left limit 3a + 1; right limit 9 - 2 = 7; existence needs 3a + 1 = 7, so a = 2. Option 2 comes from using x^2 rather than x^2 - 2 on the right, giving 3a + 1 = 9. Option 3 is a sign slip in solving 3a = 6. Option 4 assumes a change of formula at a point must always break the limit, when matching the two one-sided values repairs it exactly.

questions.q: lim as x -> 0 of (e^x - 1 - x)/x^2 equals:
options: it does not exist
questions.concept: repeated L'Hopital with the form re-checked
questions.why: At x = 0 the form is 0/0; differentiating numerator and denominator separately gives (e^x - 1)/(2x), still 0/0; differentiating again gives e^x/2 -> 1/2. Option 2 stops after one application and uses lim e^x = 1. Option 1 stops after one application and reads 0/0 as 0. Option 4 reads the repeated indeterminate form as failure. A further hidden error to avoid is differentiating with the quotient rule; the rule differentiates top and bottom separately and is not about (f/g) prime.

questions.q: (explain why) Evaluate lim as x -> 1 of (x - 1)/(sqrt(x) - 1), showing every step and naming the technique. Say why direct substitution alone is not enough.
questions.concept: conjugate rationalisation of a surd denominator
questions.why: Substitution gives (1 - 1)/(1 - 1) = 0/0, which is indeterminate and yields no value; it tells you only that (x - 1) and (sqrt(x) - 1) share a vanishing factor. Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate sqrt(x) + 1: the denominator becomes (sqrt(x) - 1)(sqrt(x) + 1) = x - 1, so the expression is (x - 1)(sqrt(x) + 1)/(x - 1) = sqrt(x) + 1 for x not equal to 1. Substituting now gives 2. Equivalently, factor the numerator as a difference of squares in sqrt(x): x - 1 = (sqrt(x) - 1)(sqrt(x) + 1), and cancel directly. The cancellation is legitimate because the limit never evaluates at x = 1.

questions.q: (explain why) Evaluate lim as x -> 2 from the left of |x - 2|/(x^2 - 4) and lim as x -> 2 from the right of |x - 2|/(x^2 - 4) separately, and state with reasons whether lim as x -> 2 of |x - 2|/(x^2 - 4) exists.
questions.concept: absolute value resolved side by side
questions.why: Factor the denominator: x^2 - 4 = (x - 2)(x + 2). From the left (x < 2): |x - 2| = -(x - 2), so the quotient is -(x - 2)/[(x - 2)(x + 2)] = -1/(x + 2) -> -1/4. From the right (x > 2): |x - 2| = x - 2, so the quotient is 1/(x + 2) -> +1/4. Both one-sided limits exist and are finite, but -1/4 is not 1/4, so the two-sided limit does not exist: a jump discontinuity. The failure is not caused by the denominator vanishing, since (x - 2) cancels on both sides; it is caused solely by the sign the absolute value contributes.

questions.q: (explain why) Evaluate lim as x -> infinity of (2x^2 - 3x + 1)/(5x^3 + x) and lim as x -> infinity of (2x^3 + 1)/(5x^2 - x), in each case by dividing through by the highest power of x, and explain what the two answers say about the graphs.
questions.concept: limits at infinity by degree comparison
questions.why: First limit: divide by x^3 to get (2/x - 3/x^2 + 1/x^3)/(5 + 1/x^2) -> 0/5 = 0, since deg N < deg D. Second limit: divide by x^3 to get (2 + 1/x^3)/(5/x - 1/x^2) -> 2/0+ = +infinity, so there is no finite limit and the function diverges, since deg N > deg D. For the graphs: the first has the horizontal asymptote y = 0 and flattens onto the x-axis far to the right; the second has no horizontal asymptote at all, and because the degrees differ by exactly one it hugs the oblique line found by long division, y = (2/5)x + 2/25. In neither case is 2/5 a horizontal asymptote; that ratio applies only when the degrees are equal.

questions.q: (explain why) A student writes: 'lim as x -> 1 of (x^2 + 3)/(x - 1) = lim as x -> 1 of 2x/1 = 2 by L'Hopital's rule.' Identify the error precisely and give the correct account of this limit.
questions.concept: entrance condition for L'Hopital's rule
questions.why: The error is at the first equality. L'Hopital's rule applies only when direct substitution gives 0/0 or infinity/infinity. Here substitution gives (1 + 3)/(1 - 1) = 4/0, which is not indeterminate but an infinite form, so the rule may not be used and its output 2 is meaningless. Correct account: the numerator tends to 4 > 0 and the denominator tends to 0, so the quotient grows without bound and the sign is decided on each side. As x -> 1 from the left, x - 1 is small negative, so the quotient -> -infinity; as x -> 1 from the right, x - 1 is small positive, so the quotient -> +infinity. The two sides disagree, so the limit does not exist and the graph has a vertical asymptote at x = 1. Check the form before every application of the rule, and again before each repeat.

checks.topic: Problems only, numerical and multi-step: emf = I(R + r) and terminal voltage, extracting emf and r from two readings, power split between load and cell, emf = Bvl with current and force, Faraday's law arithmetic, U = 1/2 C V^2, C = epsilon-0 A/d, and energy density times volume

questions.q: A cell of emf 12 V and internal resistance 2.0 ohm is connected across a 10 ohm resistor. The terminal potential difference is:
questions.concept: internal resistance goes into the total before dividing
questions.why: I = emf/(R + r) = 12/12 = 1.0 A, so V = IR = 10 V (equally emf - Ir = 12 - 2.0). Option a ignores the internal resistance and quotes the emf, correct only at zero current. Option c comes from computing I = emf/R = 1.2 A, forgetting r in the denominator, then subtracting Ir = 2.4 V - the fault is in the current, not the subtraction. Option d quotes the lost volts Ir = 2.0 V instead of what is left after them.

questions.q: A cell drives 2.0 A through a 5.0 ohm resistor, and 1.0 A through an 11.0 ohm resistor. Its emf and internal resistance are:
options: emf = 11 V, r = 1.0 ohm
emf = 12 V, r = 1.0 ohm
emf = 12 V, r = 6.0 ohm
emf = 10 V, r = 0 ohm
questions.concept: two readings, two unknowns in emf = I(R + r)
questions.why: 2.0(5.0 + r) = 1.0(11.0 + r) gives 10 + 2r = 11 + r, so r = 1.0 ohm and emf = 2.0(6.0) = 12 V. Option a takes the second terminal voltage V = IR = 11 V and calls it the emf; that is V, and emf = V + Ir = 12 V. Option c gets the emf right but reports the total resistance R + r = 6.0 ohm as the internal resistance. Option d uses only the first reading, V = 10 V, and concludes r = 0, but a single reading cannot separate emf from r, which is why two are given.

questions.q: A cell of emf 12 V and internal resistance 1.0 ohm drives a 5.0 ohm resistor. The rate at which energy is wasted inside the cell is:
questions.concept: power wasted internally is I^2 r
questions.why: I = 12/6.0 = 2.0 A, so I^2 r = (4.0)(1.0) = 4.0 W. Option a is the total power the source delivers, emf x I = 24 W, the sum of what the load gets and what is wasted. Option b is the power in the external resistor, I^2 R = 20 W, the useful part rather than the wasted part. Option d computes Ir = 2.0, which is the lost volts, and reads volts as watts. Note that 20 + 4 = 24 confirms the split.

questions.q: A rod of length 0.50 m slides at 4.0 m/s along rails in a perpendicular field of 0.30 T. The total circuit resistance is 0.60 ohm. The current in the circuit is:
questions.concept: motional emf then Ohm's law
questions.why: emf = Bvl = (0.30)(4.0)(0.50) = 0.60 V, so I = 0.60/0.60 = 1.0 A. Option a drops the length: Bv = 1.2 V gives 2.0 A. Option d drops the speed: Bl = 0.15 V gives 0.25 A. Option c is the numerical value of the emf carried over as though it were the current, the division by R having been skipped because the two numbers look alike.

questions.q: A coil of 500 turns and area 4.0 x 10^-3 m^2 lies perpendicular to a field that falls uniformly from 0.80 T to zero in 0.20 s. The magnitude of the induced emf is:
questions.concept: Faraday's law arithmetic, N A dB/dt
questions.why: dB/dt = 0.80/0.20 = 4.0 T/s; A(dB/dt) = 1.6 x 10^-2 Wb/s; times 500 turns gives 8.0 V. Option c omits the division by the time and computes N A dB = 1.6. Option d omits the number of turns, giving the emf of a single loop. Option a omits the area, computing N(dB/dt) = 2.0 x 10^3, which is not even a voltage dimensionally.

questions.q: A 20 micro-F capacitor is charged to 300 V. The energy stored is:
questions.concept: U = 1/2 C V^2 with V squared
questions.why: 1/2 (20 x 10^-6)(300)^2 = 1/2 (20 x 10^-6)(9.0 x 10^4) = 0.90 J. Option a drops the 1/2 and gives C V^2 = QV = 1.8 J, which is the work done by the battery, exactly twice what is stored. Option c halves twice, from starting with 1/2 C V^2 and then applying the 1/2 of Q^2/(2C) as well. Option d forgets to square V, computing 1/2 C V = 3.0 x 10^-3.

questions.q: A parallel-plate capacitor in vacuum has plate area 0.020 m^2 and plate separation 5.0 mm. Its capacitance is (epsilon-0 = 8.85 x 10^-12 F/m):
questions.concept: C = epsilon-0 A/d with d in metres
questions.why: (8.85 x 10^-12)(0.020)/(5.0 x 10^-3) = 3.54 x 10^-11 F. Option c leaves d in millimetres, dividing by 5.0 instead of 5.0 x 10^-3, so the answer is 10^3 times too small. Option d multiplies by d instead of dividing by it. Option b inverts the fraction inside, using d/A rather than A/d.

questions.q: In the capacitor of the previous question the field between the plates is 200 N/C. The total energy stored is:
questions.concept: total energy is energy density times the volume between the plates
questions.why: u = 1/2 epsilon-0 E^2 = 1/2 (8.85 x 10^-12)(4.0 x 10^4) = 1.77 x 10^-7 J/m^3; volume = A d = (0.020)(5.0 x 10^-3) = 1.0 x 10^-4 m^3; U = 1.77 x 10^-11 J. Cross-check: V = Ed = 1.0 V and 1/2 C V^2 with C = 3.54 x 10^-11 F gives the same. Option d is the density itself quoted as an energy, the mistake printed in this week's slides. Option c multiplies by the plate area but not the separation, so it is out by a factor of d. Option a drops the 1/2 from the density.

questions.q: A cell of emf 6.0 V and internal resistance 0.50 ohm drives a 2.5 ohm resistor. Calculate the current, the terminal potential difference, the power delivered to the resistor and the power wasted inside the cell. Show that the two powers add to emf x I, and say what emf x I represents.
questions.concept: current, terminal voltage and the power split in a real cell
questions.why: Total resistance R + r = 3.0 ohm, so I = emf/(R + r) = 6.0/3.0 = 2.0 A. Terminal pd V = IR = 5.0 V (check: emf - Ir = 6.0 - 1.0 = 5.0 V). Power to the resistor P_R = I^2 R = (4.0)(2.5) = 10 W; power wasted inside P_r = I^2 r = (4.0)(0.50) = 2.0 W. Their sum is 12 W, and emf x I = (6.0)(2.0) = 12 W. emf x I is the total rate at which the source converts chemical energy into electrical energy - the whole power output of the cell. Of it, I^2 R is delivered usefully to the external circuit and I^2 r is dissipated as heat inside the cell itself, which is what makes a cell warm and why the terminal voltage sags under load. Dividing throughout by I gives emf = V + Ir, the same statement per coulomb rather than per second.

questions.q: Two 6.0 micro-F capacitors are connected across a 20 V supply, first in parallel and then in series. Calculate the energy stored in each arrangement, and explain from the formula why one arrangement stores more than the other.
questions.concept: at fixed supply voltage the stored energy is proportional to capacitance
questions.why: Parallel: C = 6.0 + 6.0 = 12 micro-F, so U = 1/2 (12 x 10^-6)(20)^2 = 1/2 (12 x 10^-6)(400) = 2.4 x 10^-3 J. Series: 1/C = 1/6.0 + 1/6.0, so C = 3.0 micro-F and U = 1/2 (3.0 x 10^-6)(400) = 6.0 x 10^-4 J. The parallel arrangement stores four times as much. The reason is in the formula: V is fixed at 20 V by the supply and appears identically in both cases, so U is proportional to C; combining capacitors in parallel adds the capacitances, giving a value larger than the largest single capacitor, while series gives a reciprocal sum, a value smaller than the smallest single one. Here 12 micro-F is four times 3.0 micro-F and the energies stand in the same ratio. Maximum energy from a set of capacitors on a given supply is therefore always obtained in parallel - the opposite of the intuition carried over from resistors.

questions.q: A rod of length 0.80 m slides at 5.0 m/s along frictionless rails in a perpendicular field of 0.40 T; the total circuit resistance is 2.0 ohm. Find the emf, the current, the force needed to keep the rod moving at constant speed, and the mechanical power supplied. Show that this equals the electrical power dissipated, and explain why it must.
questions.concept: motional emf and the mechanical to electrical power balance
questions.why: emf = Bvl = (0.40)(5.0)(0.80) = 1.6 V. Current I = emf/R = 1.6/2.0 = 0.80 A. The field exerts a retarding force on the current-carrying rod, F = BIl = (0.40)(0.80)(0.80) = 0.256 N, so the agent must push with 0.256 N to keep the speed constant. Mechanical power P = Fv = (0.256)(5.0) = 1.28 W. Electrical power dissipated I^2 R = (0.64)(2.0) = 1.28 W (or emf^2/R = 2.56/2.0 = 1.28 W). They must be equal: the magnetic force on a charge is perpendicular to that charge's velocity and does no work, so the field supplies no energy and only separates charge to set up the emf. The sole energy input is the agent pushing the rod, and since the rod moves at constant speed its kinetic energy is not changing, so every joule supplied must reappear in the resistor. Algebraically Fv = (BIl)v = I(Bvl) = I x emf = I^2 R.

questions.q: A 50 micro-F capacitor in a defibrillator is charged to 4.0 kV and then delivers 80% of its stored energy in 5.0 ms. Find the charge on the plates, the energy stored, the energy delivered and the average power delivered. Then explain why the battery had to do more than that stored energy in charging it, and say how much more.
questions.concept: Q = CV, U = 1/2 C V^2, average power, and the factor of two in the battery's work
questions.why: Charge Q = CV = (50 x 10^-6)(4.0 x 10^3) = 0.20 C. Energy stored U = 1/2 C V^2 = 1/2 (50 x 10^-6)(1.6 x 10^7) = 400 J (check: 1/2 QV = 1/2 (0.20)(4000) = 400 J). Energy delivered = 0.80 x 400 = 320 J. Average power = 320/(5.0 x 10^-3) = 6.4 x 10^4 W = 64 kW - the point of the design, since 320 J is modest but releasing it in 5 ms gives an enormous power. The battery moves the total charge 0.20 C through its own fixed terminal voltage of 4.0 kV, so it does W = QV = 800 J, twice the 400 J stored. The reason is that the capacitor's voltage climbs from 0 to 4.0 kV as charge accumulates, so each coulomb ends up stored at an average potential of only V/2, giving 1/2 QV, whereas the battery always supplies at the full V. The difference, 400 J, is dissipated as heat in the resistance of the charging circuit - which is exactly why U = 1/2 C V^2 carries a factor of 1/2 while the battery's work QV does not.

checks.topic: Applying the approaches to stated problems: merge sort and backtracking traces, brute-force counting, greedy activity selection, pipelines, memoisation and a p-value decision

questions.q: A team must performance-test a new exam-registration portal. Which plan follows the course's method?
options: Release it to a small group of students, collect their complaints for two weeks, then fix whatever gets reported
Mine the previous portal's server logs for patterns and predict from them where the new portal is likely to fail
Write test scenarios with success criteria, then measure the portal against them using erroneous data and simulated load
Run the portal against every possible combination of input values until one of the combinations produces an error
questions.concept: performance testing carried out as specified
questions.why: The method is to come up with a set of test scenarios and success criteria and then measure the performance of the system or program against them, and the course's own scenarios are testing with erroneous data to check error handling and simulating real-life circumstances (stress testing). Option a is the timing error: performance testing happens before release, and complaints after release abandon the pre-written criteria that make it a measurement. Option b substitutes data mining for testing the artefact itself. Option d substitutes brute force, which is neither scenario-based nor feasible.

questions.q: You have forgotten the combination of a padlock with 4 wheels, each carrying the digits 0-9. How many combinations must a brute-force attack be prepared to try, and what does that number show?
options: 40 - each of the four wheels is turned through its ten digits, so the work is simple and consistent but slow
24 - the four digits of the true combination are permuted, which is why brute force is described as very slow
5000 - on average only half the space is examined, which is why brute force is called simple and consistent
10000 - every possibility is tried in turn, which is why brute force is simple and consistent but very slow
questions.concept: sizing a brute-force search space
questions.why: Four wheels of ten digits chosen independently give 10 x 10 x 10 x 10 = 10000, and brute force goes through all possible choices until a solution is found, which is why the course calls it simple and consistent but very slow. Option a is the additive error, adding 10 four times instead of multiplying, treating the wheels as if only one moved at a time. Option b treats the digits as a permutation of a fixed set (4! = 24), but digits may repeat and come from ten values. Option c uses a true remark about the average case to draw a false conclusion: brute force must still be prepared for all 10000, and the option also attaches the average to the wrong property.

questions.q: A maze is represented as a binary search tree. A solver goes left at every junction and arrives at a leaf that is a dead end. What does a backtracking algorithm do next?
options: Record the dead end so that no later path recomputes it, and then continue forward from that leaf
Return to the most recent junction that still has an option not yet tried, and follow that option instead
Begin again at the entrance of the maze, this time going right at every junction it encounters
Take, from all the leaves still unvisited, the one lying closest to the exit and continue from there
questions.concept: the backtracking move on a rejected state
questions.why: On reaching a final state the algorithm checks whether it is accepted or rejected and then backtracks to a previous state to try other unconsidered options, so a rejected leaf sends the search back to the nearest junction with an untried branch. Option a grafts dynamic programming's memoisation onto backtracking, and continuing forward from a dead end is impossible anyway. Option c is the misunderstanding that backtracking means restarting, which discards all the work above the failed junction, exactly the waste backtracking avoids. Option d is a greedy rule and also proposes a jump between leaves the tree does not permit.

questions.q: A program must produce the total cost of an order by adding up the product costs and then adding VAT. Which arrangement is pipelining as the course defines it?
options: The sum of the product costs is computed, and that result is passed to the process that adds VAT
The sum of the product costs and the VAT total are worked out separately and are added together at the end
The order is split into two halves, each half is costed on its own, and the two subtotals are then combined
The subtotal of every earlier order is stored, so that a repeat of the same order needs no recomputation
questions.concept: pipelining as a chain of processes
questions.why: The definition is that the task is divided into a series of subtasks each leading to the next, each executed by a different process, with the result of one process feeding into the next; handing the subtotal to the VAT step is the course's own order-total example. Option b is the commonest error: two computations run side by side and added at the end are independent, so nothing feeds anything, which is parallel work and not a pipeline. Option c is divide and conquer, splitting into like parts that are solved separately and combined. Option d is dynamic programming, storing results so nothing is recomputed.

questions.q: A student computes Fibonacci numbers with fib(n) = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2) and no storage; computing fib(6) this way calls fib(3) three times. Applying the course's dynamic programming to this code means:
options: splitting each call into fib(n-1) and fib(n-2) and solving each of those two independently
trying every pair of earlier terms in the sequence until a pair is found that sums to the required term
computing every term from fib(0) to fib(6) first and then selecting the largest one that is needed
storing each fib(k) the first time it is computed and reading the stored value back on later calls
questions.concept: memoisation is what dynamic programming adds
questions.why: Dynamic programming breaks a problem into sub-problems and saves the solutions of the sub-problems so there is no need to compute the result again; here the first call to fib(3) computes and stores it and the later calls read it back, so the repeated work vanishes. Option a is the sharpest distractor because it is what the code already does: splitting is plain divide and conquer without storage, exactly the situation described, so choosing it means confusing splitting with storing. Option b is brute force over pairs of terms. Option c mixes a bottom-up table with a greedy 'take the largest' step that has no meaning here, since the term needed is fixed by n.

questions.q: Six activities have start times 2, 4, 1, 6, 9, 6 and finish times 3, 5, 7, 8, 10, 10 respectively, and you cannot work on two at once. Applying the greedy rule - repeatedly take the activity finishing earliest among those starting after the last one taken - gives which schedule?
options: (1,7), (9,10) - two activities
(2,3), (4,5), (6,10) - three activities
questions.concept: running the greedy activity-selection rule
questions.why: Pairing the times gives (2,3), (4,5), (1,7), (6,8), (9,10), (6,10). Take (2,3), finishing at 3; the earliest finisher starting at or after 3 is (4,5); after 5 the earliest finisher available is (6,8), since (1,7) started at 1; after 8 only (9,10) remains. That is four activities. Option a is the earliest-start-first rule: taking (1,7) blocks both (2,3) and (4,5) and leaves room only for (9,10), the standard demonstration that the greedy criterion must be finish time. Option b chooses (6,10) over (6,8) among the two starting at 6, and the later finish then blocks (9,10). Option d ignores the no-overlap constraint, since (6,8) and (6,10) cannot both be worked.

questions.q: A hall must be wired so that every room is powered using the least total length of cable. Reduced to a more general case, the way the course reduces a building's power cable infrastructure, this problem becomes:
options: the shortest path between two rooms of the hall, found by applying Dijkstra's algorithm
a list of the rooms sorted by their distance from the meter, then wired in that sorted order
every possible wiring layout enumerated in turn, with the shortest layout among them kept
the minimum spanning tree of a graph whose vertices are rooms and whose edges are cable runs
questions.concept: reducing a problem to a more general case
questions.why: The course's own example is that an algorithm to optimise the power cable infrastructure of a building reduces to determining the minimum spanning tree of a given graph: every room must be reached, connections have lengths, and the least total length connecting everything without redundancy is a spanning tree of minimum weight. Option a is the Dijkstra confusion, since a shortest path connects two points while the requirement is to reach all rooms; the Dijkstra picture in the notes belongs to visualisation. Option b is a greedy rule applied to the wrong quantity, distance from the meter rather than the cost of runs between rooms. Option c is brute force, which abandons the reduction that problem recognition exists to find.

questions.q: A test is run at a significance level of 0.05 and the data give a p-value of 0.03. What follows, on the course's rule?
options: The null hypothesis is accepted, because a p-value as small as 0.03 is evidence in favour of the null
The null hypothesis is rejected, because the p-value is less than or equal to the significance level
The null hypothesis is rejected, and this proves that the two methods being compared are genuinely different
Nothing follows yet, because the significance level must first be lowered below the p-value obtained
questions.concept: applying the accept/reject rule
questions.why: The rule is that when the p-value is less than or equal to the significance level the null hypothesis is rejected, and when it is higher the null is accepted; 0.03 is less than 0.05, so the null is rejected. Option a inverts the meaning of the p-value, since the smaller it is the stronger the evidence to reject, and this is the commonest error on the topic. Option c gets the decision right but overclaims: the course states that rejecting the null does not prove something does not exist, only that the evidence is not enough, and a rejection at 0.05 carries a 5 percent risk of being made when the null is true. Option d reverses the comparison, since the significance level is fixed in advance.

questions.q: Sort 2, 8, 4, 9, 3 into descending order using merge sort, writing out every split and every merge, and showing the individual comparisons made during the final merge. Then say which of divide and conquer's two conditions the algorithm relies on when it claims the merge step was worth the split.
questions.concept: tracing merge sort and the condition that justifies the merge
questions.why: Split: [2, 8, 4, 9, 3] divides into [2, 8] and [4, 9, 3]; [2, 8] divides into [2] and [8]; [4, 9, 3] divides into [4] and [9, 3], and [9, 3] divides into [9] and [3]. Single elements are already sorted, the base case, so the parts have become simpler than the whole. Merge descending, always taking the larger head: [2] with [8] gives 8 then 2, that is [8, 2]; [9] with [3] gives [9, 3]; [4] with [9, 3] compares 4 against 9 to take 9, then 4 against 3 to take 4, then 3, giving [9, 4, 3]. Final merge of [8, 2] with [9, 4, 3]: 8 against 9 takes 9; 8 against 4 takes 8; 2 against 4 takes 4; 2 against 3 takes 3; the left list is exhausted so 2 is appended. Result [9, 8, 4, 3, 2]. Descending order is produced inside the merge by taking the larger head each time, not by sorting ascending and reversing afterwards. The condition relied on is the second: divide and conquer is worth using only when combining the solutions of the smaller parts is less complicated than solving the original problem directly (the companion condition being that the parts be genuinely simpler than the whole). Merging two sorted lists needs only one comparison per element placed, because each list's largest remaining element sits at its head, which is cheaper than sorting the original list directly, and that is what makes the split pay.

questions.q: A food delivery service in a busy city wants to minimise delivery times and fuel costs across many drivers and many orders. Set out one greedy step sequence and one divide-and-conquer step sequence for this problem. For the divide-and-conquer plan, state the condition it must satisfy to be worth using here. For the greedy plan, give a concrete arrangement of orders on which it returns a route that is not optimal, and say why the greedy rule cannot detect that.
questions.concept: applying greedy and divide and conquer to the delivery-routing case study
questions.why: Greedy sequence: start each driver at the restaurant with a list of undelivered orders; from the current position compute the travel time to every undelivered order; go to the nearest one, the best possible choice available at this stage; mark it delivered and repeat until the list is empty. This applies the best option at each stage, is simple and highly efficient to compute, and needs no view of the whole route. Divide-and-conquer sequence: split the city into zones, say four quadrants, so each zone holds a manageable set of orders; split further any zone still holding too many; solve each small zone by finding a good route through its own orders; combine the zone routes by ordering the zones and joining each zone's exit point to the next zone's entry point, giving a route for the whole city. The condition: routing one zone must genuinely be simpler than routing the whole city, and joining the zone routes must be less complicated than routing the city directly. That fails if zone boundaries cut through clusters of orders, since the joins then criss-cross the city and cost more than they saved. Where greedy is not optimal: a busy city has one-way streets, so travel times are not symmetric. Take two orders A and B. From the restaurant A is 2 minutes away and B is 5 minutes away; because of a one-way ring, A to B takes 12 minutes while B to A takes only 3; the return legs are A to restaurant 2 minutes and B to restaurant 5. Greedy takes the best option at this stage, A at 2 minutes, and is then committed to the 12-minute leg and a 5-minute return, 19 minutes in all, whereas delivering B first costs 5 + 3 + 2 = 10 minutes. The greedy rule cannot detect this because at each stage it compares only the legs leading out of where it now stands; it never prices the remainder of the route, so it cannot see that paying 3 extra minutes on the first leg buys 9 back on the second. This is the course's caveat that greedy might not always produce an optimal solution, while remaining simple and highly efficient wherever it does.

questions.q: Write the order-total task of question 4 out as a pipeline of at least four subtasks, naming each subtask's input and output. Then state what makes this a pipeline rather than merely a list of steps, and explain what happens to the pipeline if one subtask's output does not match the next subtask's expected input.
questions.concept: laying out a pipeline and the dependency that defines it
questions.why: Subtask 1, collect line items: input the order id, output a list of (product, quantity) pairs. Subtask 2, price the line items: input that list, output a list of line costs (unit price times quantity). Subtask 3, sum the line costs: input the list of line costs, output one number, the subtotal. Subtask 4, compute VAT: input the subtotal, output the VAT amount. Subtask 5, add VAT to the subtotal: input subtotal and VAT amount, output the total cost. A sixth stage formatting the total as currency is a legitimate final stage. What makes it a pipeline: each subtask is executed by a different process in a series and the result of one process is the input of the next, so subtask 3 cannot start until subtask 2 has produced its list and subtask 4 cannot start until the subtotal exists. A mere list of steps has an order in which someone happens to do things; a pipeline has an order forced by the data, because each stage consumes what the previous stage produced, repeated until the whole task is completed. If an output does not match the next input, the chain breaks at that junction and everything downstream is wrong or cannot run: if subtask 3 hands on a list instead of a single number, the VAT stage has nothing to multiply; if subtask 4 emits a percentage rate rather than an amount, subtask 5 adds 7.5 to the subtotal instead of 7.5 per cent of it and the total is silently wrong. Because the stages are chained rather than independent, a fault at any stage propagates to the end, which is why a pipeline is tested stage by stage, checking each stage's output against the next stage's expected input.

questions.q: A team proposes a program that will predict, for every road junction in Lagos, the exact traffic one week ahead, using every GPS ping recorded by every delivery vehicle over the last ten years. Work the proposal through the course's three factors in order, say which factor it fails on first and why, and state one change that would let it pass.
questions.concept: applying the three factors that gate computational approaches
questions.why: Factor one, is the problem clearly defined? Only partly. The current situation (ten years of GPS pings) and the end goal (traffic at every junction one week ahead) are stated, but 'exact traffic' is not a defined quantity (vehicles per hour? queue length?) and no obstacles have been identified, so how the end goal is to be reached is unstated; this is weak but repairable. Factor two, is the problem computable? This is where the proposal fails first and hardest. The factor asks whether the required calculations are possible considering processing times and capacity, and predicting the exact state of every junction a week ahead is not a calculation completable to that standard by any amount of processing, because traffic depends on weather, incidents and human choices not present in the data; the demand is impossible in kind, not merely expensive. Factor three, have the data requirements been examined? They have not: every GPS ping from every vehicle over ten years is a big data volume whose data types and storage capacity have not been identified, and no plan for storing or moving it is named. The change: replace the exact one-week-ahead target with a bounded, computable one, for example predict the average congestion band (light, moderate, heavy) at the fifty busiest junctions for each hour of the next day, using pings from the last two years sampled to a stated resolution. That makes the goal definite, brings the calculation inside realistic processing times and capacity, and lets the data types and storage be specified, after which the machine learning and statistical analysis techniques of data mining are the right instrument for the retained data.

recapCandidates.topic: Indeterminate forms - reading the shape of a limit and choosing the technique it demands
recapCandidates.whyMisunderstood: Students learn the four techniques - substitute, factor, conjugate, divide by the highest power - as four disconnected recipes and then guess between them under pressure instead of diagnosing the limit first. The diagnosis turns on one distinction almost nobody states cleanly: 0/0 is indeterminate, but c/0 with c not zero is not. The first means the algebra is hiding a cancellation; the second means the limit is plus or minus infinity and each side must be checked separately. A student who blurs them either writes 'does not exist' for a perfectly good 0/0 limit or writes 'infinity' for one that was 0/0 all along. Underneath sits a second confusion: substituting to get 0/0 does not show the limit fails to exist - substitution is only a test, and its failure means the limit laws' hypotheses were not met. A third layer is the belief that the limit and the function value are the same thing, so a hole makes the limit undefined; the definition explicitly excludes x = a, which is exactly why limits see past holes. Finally students reach for L'Hopital's rule as a first move rather than a last one, and then differentiate the quotient with the quotient rule, when differentiating numerator and denominator separately is the whole point of the rule.
whyQuestions: Why is 0/0 called indeterminate while 5/0 is not - what different thing is each one telling you to do next?
Why does the definition of a limit deliberately exclude x = a, and why does that make the limit of (x^2 - 4)/(x - 2) as x -> 2 equal to 4 even though the function is undefined at 2?
Why does multiplying by the conjugate remove a 0/0 in (sqrt(x+4) - 2)/x, when it looks like it only makes the expression bigger?
Why do you divide by the highest power in the denominator for a limit at infinity, and why does that rule turn into 'compare the degrees' for a rational function?
Why does substitution giving 0/0 fail to prove that the limit does not exist, and what is the only thing that ever proves a two-sided limit does not exist?
