recapCandidates.goodAnswerContains: Names the diagnosis step first: always substitute; a number is the limit, 0/0 means a removable common factor needs algebra, and c/0 with c non-zero means the answer is plus or minus infinity with each side checked by sign. Matches shape to technique and says why each works: polynomials -> factor and cancel the (x - a) that caused the 0/0; surds -> conjugate, because (sqrt(A) - B)(sqrt(A) + B) = A - B^2 kills the root; stacked fractions -> common denominator; x -> infinity -> divide by the highest power and use 1/x^n -> 0. States the only existence test - both one-sided limits must exist and be equal - and that the limit is about approach, never about f(a), so a hole is invisible to it.
recapCandidates.workedExample: (a) Limit of (x^2 - 9)/(x^2 - x - 6) as x -> 3. Substituting gives 0/0, indeterminate, so factor: (x-3)(x+3)/((x-3)(x+2)). Cancel the (x-3), legitimate because x is never equal to 3 in the limit process, leaving (x+3)/(x+2), which now takes substitution: 6/5. (b) Limit of (sqrt(x+9) - 3)/x as x -> 0. Substituting gives 0/0. Multiply top and bottom by the conjugate (sqrt(x+9) + 3): the numerator becomes (x+9) - 9 = x, so the quotient is 1/(sqrt(x+9)+3), and substituting gives 1/6. (c) Limit of (x+1)/(x-2) as x -> 2. Substituting gives 3/0, which is NOT indeterminate, so no algebra will help. Check sides: as x -> 2 from the left the top -> 3 > 0 and the bottom -> 0 from below, so f -> minus infinity; from the right f -> plus infinity. The two-sided limit does not exist, and the honest answer says so and gives both one-sided behaviours. (d) Limit of (3x^2 - x)/(5x^2 + 4) as x -> infinity. Substituting gives infinity/infinity. Divide top and bottom by x^2: (3 - 1/x)/(5 + 4/x^2). Every 1/x^n -> 0, so the limit is 3/5 - the ratio of leading coefficients, which is the Week 2 degree rule falling out of the same manoeuvre. Note what (a) and (c) share and where they part: both have a zero denominator at the target, and only factoring reveals which is which.

recapCandidates.topic: emf versus terminal potential difference - what internal resistance actually does
recapCandidates.whyMisunderstood: The name is the first trap: electromotive force is not a force, it is work per unit charge measured in volts, and a student who carries the word 'force' into the problem starts reaching for newtons. The second and costlier trap is treating emf and terminal voltage as two names for the same quantity. They are equal in exactly one situation - no current flowing - and every closed-circuit question hinges on their being different. A student who writes V = emf with the switch closed loses the whole question, and one who knows emf = V + Ir often still cannot say what the Ir term physically is: energy the cell spends heating itself, which never reaches the load. The third layer is direction of change. Because I = emf/(R + r), lowering the external resistance raises the current and therefore raises the lost volts, so terminal voltage falls as you demand more from the cell - which is why a torch dims when the battery is old and why a short circuit gives maximum current and near-zero terminal voltage. Students routinely predict this backwards. The fourth is the graph: in the V-I experiment the line has intercept emf and gradient minus r, and that minus sign is the statement that terminal voltage falls off with current, not a convention to be ignored.
whyQuestions: Why is emf measured in volts and not in newtons, and what exactly is the 'work per unit charge' being counted?
Why does the voltmeter read the full emf on an open circuit but less than the emf the moment the switch closes?
Why does decreasing the external resistance R make the terminal voltage V go down, when the cell has not changed at all?
Why is the gradient of the V-against-I graph equal to minus r rather than plus r, and why does the intercept give the emf?
Why does an old battery still show nearly its full rated voltage on a multimeter yet fail to run a motor - and what has actually changed inside it?
recapCandidates.goodAnswerContains: Defines emf = W/Q as the energy in joules the source gives to each coulomb it drives round the circuit (unit V = J/C), and V as the potential difference across the terminals while current flows, equal to IR. Derives rather than quotes: the emf per coulomb is split between the external circuit and the cell's own resistance, so emf = V + Ir = I(R + r), hence V = emf - Ir, with V = emf only when I = 0; in power terms emf times I = I^2 R + I^2 r, the second term being heat wasted inside the cell. Reads the consequences off those equations: smaller R -> larger I -> larger lost volts -> smaller V; short circuit (R -> 0) gives I max = emf/r with V -> 0; and V = emf - rI is a straight line of intercept emf and gradient minus r.
recapCandidates.workedExample: A cell of emf 1.5 V and internal resistance 0.50 ohm is connected to an external resistor R. With R = 4.0 ohm: I = 1.5/4.5 = 0.333 A; lost volts Ir = 0.167 V, so V = 1.5 - 0.167 = 1.33 V. Power to the load I^2 R = 0.444 W; power wasted in the cell I^2 r = 0.056 W; total emf times I = 0.50 W, which checks. With R = 1.0 ohm: I = 1.5/1.5 = 1.0 A, Ir = 0.50 V, so V = 1.0 V - the terminal voltage has fallen by a third because the current tripled. Short circuit (R = 0): I = 1.5/0.50 = 3.0 A and V = 0 V, with all 4.5 W dissipated inside the cell. Getting emf and r from two readings: the pairs (I, V) = (0.333, 1.33) and (1.0, 1.0) give gradient (1.0 - 1.33)/(1.0 - 0.333) = -0.50, so r = 0.50 ohm; extrapolating to I = 0 gives V = 1.5 V = the emf. That is the whole V-I experiment in two points: intercept emf, gradient minus r. An old battery is a cell whose r has grown to several ohms: on a multimeter almost no current flows so V is close to the emf and the reading looks fine, but under a real load the Ir term eats nearly the whole emf.
